catalog_quote: Matters of juncture, stress, and intonation ... are not of concern in this discussion. ... [2.2] the phonological word is the unit of stress placement in the phonological hierarchy. Each phonological word has one and only one stress. The factors that condition stress have not been studied and, as mentioned, are not the concern of this discussion. It is clear, however, that stress is neither contrastive nor used at all in connection with semantic emphasis in Dinka. The final margin of the phonological word is characterized by potential pause. ... one syllable is stressed in each word. ... [2.3] the syllable in Dinka is the unit of tone placement. Every syllable carries one and only one tone.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: Described in terms of the elements distributed in it and the features which characterize it, the phonological word is the unit of stress placement in the phonological hierarchy. Each phonological word has one and only one stress. The factors that condition stress have not been studied and, as mentioned, are not the concern of this discussion. It is clear, however, that stress is neither contrastive nor used at all in connection with semantic emphasis in Dinka. The final margin of the phonological word is characterized by potential pause. The phonological word is the level of distribution of the syllable: one syllable is stressed in each word.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Dinka is a tone language (tone, vowel length and voice quality are the contrastive suprasegmentals). Malou states that every phonological word carries exactly one stress, that stress is not contrastive and not used for emphasis, and that what conditions its placement has not been studied; no positional rule is given (his examples in (5) mark stress on various syllables). Later work on other dialects either finds no acoustic support for stress (Remijsen & Gilley 2008 on Luanyjang, per Remijsen & Manyang 2009 fn.5) or says Dinka 'lacks an obvious stress system' (van Urk & Chong 2025).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned; one stress per phonological word.
new_statements.exceptions: None; placement conditions explicitly left unstudied. Gilley 2003 (not read) reportedly treats the morphological short grade of stems as '+stress', a different, morphological use of the term.
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word (a unit bounded by potential pause; may contain several grammatical words, cf. examples (5) such as aca yat 'I have taken it'), citation-style elicited material. Statement is pan-Dinka, not specific to Northwestern Dinka.
new_statements.identity_note: Northwestern Dinka [diw] / nort2816 = Ruweng (Pan-Aru, Alor, Paweny) plus Ngok-Kordofan (Abyei), per the Roettger & Roettger 1989 and Blench 2005 lgcodes in Glottolog's hh.bib; Glottolog lists no child dialects and the alt name Ruweng. No first-hand description of any of these varieties was found. The quoted statement (Malou 1988) is a pan-Dinka analysis by a native speaker whose own variety is not stated; p.1 names the four varieties covered as Eastern (Bor-based), Northern (Padang, Dongjol-based; = nort2815), Southern (Agar) and Western (Rek) and asserts one analysis covers 'the whole Dinka language'. Ruweng is traditionally grouped with Padang/Northern Dinka (Tucker & Bryan; Ethnologue later split dip/diw), so the statement plausibly extends to nort2816 but does not name it. Blum 2023's Ngok chapter is Ngok-Sobat (nort2815), not Abyei Ngok. The same Malou statement is already the record for sout2834 and nort2815; a reviewer may prefer a family-level (Dinka) entry over repeating it under each ISO code.

sources.note: Nothing on stress ('stress' only in reference titles). Ruweng is mentioned only second-hand via Remijsen 2010 (TIE4 slides): Ruweng shows Dissimilatory Lowering (p.112) and has 'likely' lost the High/Fall contrast (three-toned like Agar). The Ngok of ch.5 is Ngok-Sobat (speakers from near Malakal) = nort2815, not Ngok-Kordofan; p.13 notes Tucker & Bryan collapsed the two Ngoks.

sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Luanyjang (Southwestern Dinka), not nort2816. fn.5 p.119: Gilley (2003) analyses the morphological short grade as '+stress' for Dinka as a whole; Remijsen & Gilley (2008) find no acoustic evidence for this in Luanyjang; 'it cannot be ruled out that Gilley's stress hypothesis would hold for other dialects'. Tone: one toneme per morpheme on the rightmost syllable; no word-stress rule.
